title: Nonsurgical therapy for hydrocephalus: a comprehensive and critical review

subsections.subsection_title: Core CSF Physiology and Brain Fluid Homeostasis
subsections.content:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis emerges from coordinated exchange among ventricular, subarachnoid, interstitial, vascular, and lymphatic compartments rather than from a single unidirectional stream. Classical work established human CSF formation rates on the order of 0.3–0.4 ml/min and linked absorption to pressure-dependent outflow, while modern syntheses emphasize that bulk secretion, diffusional exchange, and pulsatile fluid motion coexist across brain barriers and perivascular pathways ref [6], ref [2], ref [4], ref [5].

The choroid plexus remains the dominant source of ventricular CSF and the principal blood-CSF barrier. Its fenestrated capillaries, tight-junctioned epithelium, and polarized transport machinery support energy-dependent movement of Na+, Cl−, and HCO3−, with water following through transcellular and possibly cotransporter-linked routes; in humans, daily CSF turnover is roughly three to four times the total CSF volume ref [1], ref [2], ref [6]. This role is conceptually important for hydrocephalus because altered transporter activity, plexus hyperplasia, or impaired outflow can all perturb intracranial volume regulation ref [1], ref [2].

At the parenchymal interface, astrocytic AQP4 enriches perivascular and subpial endfeet, facilitating bidirectional water exchange, extracellular volume regulation, and clearance of interstitial solutes, whereas AQP1 is concentrated in choroid plexus epithelium ref [3], ref [2]. Contemporary models therefore view CSF dynamics as a hybrid system: net choroidal secretion is superimposed on cardiac- and respiration-driven oscillatory flow, capillary-interstitial water exchange, and perivascular transport whose magnitude and direction remain debated ref [4], ref [5]. This more distributed framework is essential for interpreting hydrocephalus pathophysiology and the limits of nonsurgical interventions aimed at modulating CSF production or brain water handling ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Hydrocephalus Classification, Clinical Scope, and Review Framing
subsections.content:
Hydrocephalus is not a single disease but a heterogeneous family of disorders defined by disturbed cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, ventricular enlargement, and context-specific brain injury. Contemporary classification has moved beyond the traditional communicating/noncommunicating dichotomy toward schemes anchored in the anatomical site of CSF flow restriction, while also incorporating etiology, chronicity, and age at presentation; this framework is particularly useful for linking mechanism, imaging phenotype, and treatment selection in both clinical and experimental studies ref [7]. Such distinctions matter because congenital aqueductal stenosis, postinfectious or posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, tumor-related obstruction, syndromic pediatric hydrocephalus, and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) differ substantially in pathogenesis, natural history, and therapeutic responsiveness ref [7], ref [8], ref [9].

The clinical scope relevant to nonsurgical therapy therefore spans neonatal, pediatric, and adult hydrocephalus, but not all forms are equally appropriate for medical intervention. In preterm infants, posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus represents a major translational target because ventricular dilation emerges in the setting of germinal matrix–intraventricular hemorrhage, inflammation, evolving white-matter vulnerability, and often a prolonged preoperative interval during which temporizing or adjunctive nonsurgical strategies may be considered ref [8]. By contrast, iNPH is clinically important not because it is primarily treated medically, but because it exemplifies a common adult hydrocephalus syndrome in which diagnosis, prognostic testing, and selection for shunting are central; evidence-based guidelines indicate that shunting is possibly effective and that physiologic tests such as elevated resistance to CSF outflow can help predict response ref [9].

Accordingly, this review frames “nonsurgical therapy” broadly but critically: it includes pharmacologic efforts to reduce CSF production, modify absorption, attenuate posthemorrhagic/inflammatory scarring, or protect the injured brain, while recognizing that many hydrocephalus subtypes remain fundamentally structural disorders for which surgery is standard of care. Classification is therefore not merely descriptive; it determines whether a candidate therapy is intended as definitive treatment, temporizing bridge, disease-modifying adjunct, or mechanism-probing experimental tool ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. This framing also explains why the strongest translational opportunities may lie less in replacing shunts universally than in subtype-specific intervention aligned to mechanism and developmental stage.

Nonsurgical therapy for hydrocephalus must be interpreted against the continuing dominance of surgery and the mechanistic heterogeneity of the disease. Even within surgical practice, outcome depends on pathophysiology: in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, evidence for endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) remains sparse and low-certainty, underscoring that communicating phenotypes are not uniformly amenable to diversion or bypass concepts developed for obstructive disease ref [11]. In infants, however, prospective data suggest that ETV combined with choroid plexus cauterization (CPC) can outperform ETV alone, especially in nonpostinfectious hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele-associated cases, thereby highlighting CSF-production control as a clinically meaningful adjunct in selected contexts ref [14].

Experimental models also show that hydrocephalus is driven not only by bulk-flow obstruction but by blood-derived injury cascades. After intraventricular hemorrhage, thrombin promotes ventricular enlargement, ependymal damage, and periventricular blood-brain barrier disruption through PAR-1-dependent signaling, linking coagulation biology to posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus and providing a mechanistic rationale for targeted pharmacologic interruption ref [13]. This disease-mechanism perspective is essential when judging medical therapies aimed at inflammation, fibrosis, ion transport, or secretory epithelium.

Historically, attempts to suppress CSF production anticipated modern pharmacologic thinking. Intraventricular radioactive gold produced selective choroid plexus necrosis with reduced CSF flow and pressure in experimental hydrocephalus, but later work showed diffuse ventricular deposition and unresolved safety concerns, limiting translational plausibility ref [8], ref [16], ref [15]. More recent immunotoxin studies similarly demonstrated efficient in-vitro killing of choroid plexus-derived cells, yet their own commentaries emphasized the enduring problem of substantial extrachoroidal CSF formation and the uncertain therapeutic value of plexus ablation alone ref [9]. Together, these surgical and experimental literatures frame nonsurgical therapy less as a replacement for established operations than as a mechanism-targeted attempt to modulate distinct hydrocephalus endotypes.

subsections.subsection_title: Historical Foundations of Medical Therapy for Hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Attempts at nonsurgical therapy for hydrocephalus predate modern shunting by decades and initially reflected a physiologic ambition: to reduce CSF formation, enhance absorption, or transiently lower intracranial pressure when surgery was hazardous or unavailable. Early reports included purine-diuretic strategies such as theobromin sodio-salicylate (diuretin), which Marriott promoted for apparently communicating hydrocephalus but not obstructive disease, illustrating from the outset the dependence of response on hydrocephalus subtype and the weak evidentiary standards of the era ref [18]. Mid-century experimental work then provided a stronger mechanistic basis for medical therapy by showing that carbonic anhydrase inhibition could suppress CSF formation and lower intracranial pressure in animals ref [12].

This experimental rationale drove clinical use of acetazolamide and related agents, but longer-term pediatric experience was mixed. Early case series suggested benefit, and reviews of the period continued to frame carbonic anhydrase inhibitors as plausible medical adjuncts ref [21], ref [14]. Yet more systematic follow-up in chronic infantile hydrocephalus found only modest mean pressure reduction with apparent escape during prolonged dosing, while later studies in infants with myelomeningocele failed to prevent progression reliably ref [14]. These disappointments redirected attention toward osmotic agents, first glycerol for acute intracranial pressure reduction ref [11], and then oral isosorbide, which was attractive because it could be administered repeatedly outside the operating room ref [22].

The isosorbide literature of the late 1960s and early 1970s represents the high-water mark of historical medical therapy for hydrocephalus. Investigators documented short-term reductions in ventricular pressure and, in selected infants, temporary slowing of head growth or CSF leakage, including in infantile hydrocephalus and myelodysplasia-associated disease ref [21], ref [22], ref [23], ref [10]. However, efficacy was inconsistent, generally better in less severe disease, frequently followed by rebound after withdrawal, and limited by hypernatremic dehydration, vomiting, poor palatability, and intensive monitoring demands ref [21], ref [22], ref [23], ref [10]. Later comparative experience in myelodysplasia was substantially less encouraging, helping explain why medical therapy remained historically important as a bridge, temporizing measure, or proof-of-concept rather than a durable alternative to surgery ref [10].

subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacologic Modulation of CSF Dynamics and Translational Evidence
subsections.content:
Pharmacologic manipulation of CSF dynamics has historically targeted choroid plexus secretion more than downstream glymphatic or absorptive pathways. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition remains the canonical strategy: experimental studies showed that acetazolamide reduces CSF formation, and combined mechanistic work with furosemide linked this effect to suppression of choroid plexus carbonic anhydrase activity and reduced CSF production ref [10]. In animal and human physiologic studies, acetazolamide lowered CSF pressure, although often incompletely and with accompanying systemic acid-base effects rather than a durable normalization of CSF homeostasis ref [26]. Furosemide likewise reduced CSF formation and intracranial pressure in experimental preparations, including neonatal models, supporting the concept that loop diuretics can influence choroid-plexus-driven secretion independent of simple dehydration ref [11]. Glucocorticoids also transiently decreased CSF flow in dogs, suggesting a broader pharmacologic space beyond diuretics, albeit with limited translational follow-through ref [16].

Yet translational evidence has been consistently disappointing. In preterm infants with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, the pivotal randomized trial of acetazolamide plus furosemide found no reduction in death-or-shunt outcomes and showed worse 1-year neurodevelopmental results, with excess nephrocalcinosis and frequent treatment-limiting biochemical toxicity ref [12]. Systematic review reached the same conclusion: diuretic therapy neither reduced shunt dependence nor improved overall outcome, while increasing adverse events ref [13]. Earlier small or uncontrolled series had suggested possible benefit, but these signals were not reproduced under randomized conditions ref [12], ref [13].

Other pharmacologic approaches have been even less convincing. Digoxin can transiently suppress CSF formation in infant rats, but the effect is brief and clinically ineffective in infants with obstructive hydrocephalus, underscoring the gap between acute secretion arrest and useful long-term disease control ref [15]. More recently, veterinary data further illustrate this translational ceiling: acetazolamide at conventional dosing failed to improve neurologic signs or ventricular volume in dogs with internal hydrocephalus, whereas subsequent shunting produced clear benefit ref [25]. Collectively, these data indicate that modest short-term suppression of CSF production is biologically real but therapeutically insufficient for established hydrocephalus, especially when ventricular enlargement is driven by hemorrhagic injury, impaired absorption, inflammation, or evolving parenchymal damage rather than secretion alone ref [25], ref [12], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Restoration of CSF Pathways and Prevention of Subarachnoid Fibrosis
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Context, Guidelines, and Broader Management of Posthemorrhagic Ventricular Dilatation
subsections.content:
Posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD) in preterm infants is a high-stakes clinical syndrome rather than a simple radiographic finding: progressive ventricular enlargement after severe intraventricular hemorrhage is associated with white-matter distortion, impaired brain growth, and substantial risks of cerebral palsy, cognitive disability, and later shunt dependence ref [33], ref [34], ref [35], ref [36]. Quantitative MRI studies further suggest that adverse outcome tracks more closely with reduced cerebral, cerebellar, and thalamic growth than with ventricular size alone, reinforcing the need for timely surveillance and intervention before prolonged secondary injury accrues ref [33].

Current management is therefore centered on structured monitoring and staged temporization. Cranial ultrasound remains the bedside standard, using ventricular index and complementary measures such as anterior horn width, third-ventricle width, and thalamo-occipital distance to identify progression; serial head circumference, fontanelle tension, neurological examination, and, in some centers, Doppler resistance indices help contextualize treatment thresholds ref [34], ref [35]. Broader evidence-based guidance supports ventricular access devices, external ventricular drains, ventriculosubgaleal shunts, or selected lumbar punctures as temporizing options, but does not endorse routine serial lumbar puncture to prevent shunting or progression ref [36]. Likewise, acetazolamide/furosemide and intraventricular thrombolytics are not recommended for reducing shunt need, and there is insufficient evidence to define a universal weight, CSF protein cutoff, or role for primary ETV; clinical judgment remains central ref [34], ref [35], ref [36].

In practice, broader PHVD management extends beyond CSF diversion decisions to prevention of secondary injury, infection control, and neurodevelopmental follow-up. Early intervention strategies may improve developmental trajectories compared with delayed drainage in some cohorts, although optimal timing remains unsettled ref [34], ref [36]. Permanent shunting is usually deferred until the infant is larger and clinically stable, yet many survivors still require long-term CSF diversion ref [34], ref [35]. This clinical context explains why restoration of CSF pathways and prevention of subarachnoid fibrosis have become attractive nonsurgical goals: they aim not merely to shrink ventricles, but to preserve brain development during a uniquely vulnerable period ref [33], ref [34], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Restoration of CSF Pathways and Prevention of Subarachnoid Fibrosis
subsections.subsection_title: Anti-fibrotic and Matrix-Modulating Approaches to Preserve CSF Circulation
subsections.content:
Anti-fibrotic strategies aim to preserve CSF circulation by interrupting the transition from hemorrhage- or inflammation-triggered meningeal injury to durable extracellular-matrix scarring. Experimental work has focused primarily on TGF-beta-centered pathways, because posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus is repeatedly associated with increased TGF-beta signaling, fibroblast activation, and deposition of fibronectin, laminin, collagen, and related matrix components that can obstruct cisternal and absorptive pathways ref [40], ref [41], ref [42].

The most persuasive preclinical anti-fibrotic signal comes from decorin, an endogenous TGF-beta antagonist. In juvenile kaolin-induced communicating hydrocephalus, continuous intraventricular decorin prevented ventriculomegaly, reduced pSmad2/3 activation, and suppressed subarachnoid laminin/fibronectin accumulation together with inflammatory cell ingress, supporting the concept that matrix modulation can preserve CSF patency when delivered early and continuously ref [41]. By contrast, oral pirfenidone and losartan, despite antifibrotic efficacy in other organs, did not reduce ventricular enlargement or motor impairment in a neonatal rat intraventricular hemorrhage model, underscoring that CNS posthemorrhagic fibrosis may not be readily tractable through indirect systemic TGF-beta suppression alone ref [40]. Heavy water likewise reduced cisternal fibrosis, fibroblast proliferation, and TGF-beta1 expression in kaolin-treated mice, but its translational relevance is limited by nonspecific biological effects and uncertain safety for clinical use ref [42].

Older anti-inflammatory work suggested that systemic corticosteroids could lower the incidence of posthemorrhagic experimental hydrocephalus, presumably by attenuating early villous and meningeal inflammatory responses, although intraventricular depot steroid delivery itself could worsen ventricular enlargement and does not constitute a viable matrix-directed therapy ref [39]. A more direct matrix-remodeling concept is enzymatic disruption of adhesive substrates: hyaluronan is a major regulator of early wound matrices and inflammatory cell trafficking ref [8], while intrathecal or intraventricular hyaluronidase was historically reported to improve tuberculous cranial arachnoiditis and communicating hydrocephalus, albeit in uncontrolled data that predate modern imaging and trial standards ref [10]. Overall, these studies support antifibrotic and matrix-modulating therapy as biologically plausible, but only decorin currently offers robust proof-of-concept for preserving CSF pathways in vivo ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Restoration of CSF Pathways and Prevention of Subarachnoid Fibrosis
subsections.subsection_title: Subarachnoid Fibrosis and TGF-beta-Driven Scarring Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Subarachnoid fibrosis after hemorrhage is a central mechanistic link between blood exposure and delayed communicating hydrocephalus. Human pathological studies show that, beyond transient mechanical obstruction by clot, arachnoid villi and leptomeninges develop inflammatory cell infiltration, arachnoid cap-cell proliferation, and architectural remodeling that can impede CSF egress; notably, this process may involve cellular hyperplasia and diffuse subarachnoid scarring more than simple villus fibrosis alone ref [44]. Earlier clinicopathological work and experimental studies similarly implicated leptomeningeal fibrosis and arachnoid-pial adhesions as contributors to chronic posthemorrhagic CSF circulation failure.

Among candidate profibrotic mediators, TGF-beta has the strongest convergent support. CSF TGF-beta1 rises after SAH and is higher in patients who later develop ventricular dilatation, periventricular change, or shunt-dependent chronic hydrocephalus ref [45], ref [46]. Subsequent work extended this association to both TGF-beta1 and TGF-beta2, with persistently elevated early CSF levels predicting chronic communicating hydrocephalus after SAH ref [49]. However, not all cohorts reproduced a direct correlation across mixed SAH/IVH populations, suggesting heterogeneity related to hemorrhage compartment, timing, and the distinction between exogenous clot-derived versus endogenous CNS sources of TGF-beta ref [49].

Experimental models provide mechanistic plausibility for causation rather than mere association. Intrathecal recombinant TGF-beta1 induces slowly progressive communicating hydrocephalus with fibroblast accumulation, collagen deposition, and disruption of the normally lamellar leptomeningeal ultrastructure ref [9]. Likewise, CNS overexpression of TGF-beta1 in transgenic mice produces hydrocephalus with excess extracellular matrix deposition ref [10], while matrix remodeling shifts toward reduced proteolysis, including altered MMP-9/TIMP-1 balance, in TGF-beta-driven disease states ref [16]. Upstream, thrombin can activate a TGF-beta1/Smad3/CTGF fibrotic cascade in meninges, further linking hemorrhage breakdown products to profibrotic remodeling of CSF pathways ref [14]. Collectively, these data support TGF-beta-centered scarring as a major therapeutic target, although pathway redundancy and inconsistent biomarker-performance across studies caution against oversimplified models.

subsections.section_title: Restoration of CSF Pathways and Prevention of Subarachnoid Fibrosis
subsections.subsection_title: Fibrinolytic Restoration of CSF Pathways After Intraventricular or Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
subsections.content:
Fibrinolytic restoration of CSF pathways after hemorrhage is conceptually attractive because early hydrocephalus after IVH or SAH is driven, at least in part, by blood clot obstruction within the ventricles, basal cisterns, and absorptive pathways. Experimental work provided the initial proof of principle: intraventricular urokinase in dogs markedly accelerated clot clearance, reduced later ventricular enlargement, and was associated with less subarachnoid fibrosis, while intracisternal rtPA in cats after SAH improved CSF outflow resistance and normalized ventricular size when given 24 hours after hemorrhage; similar benefits were reported in pig IVH models assessing CSF dynamics after fibrinolysis ref [53], ref [54], ref [55].

Translation to neonates has been mixed. Pilot intraventricular fibrinolysis studies with streptokinase, urokinase, or rtPA suggested technical feasibility and occasional avoidance of shunt dependence, but also highlighted important limitations, including rebleeding risk, variable clot response, and uncertain efficacy when treatment is initiated after PHVD is already established ref [9], ref [10]. A mechanistic explanation is that CSF plasminogen concentrations after neonatal IVH are extremely low, potentially limiting clot lysis even when exogenous plasminogen activators are delivered ref [58]. This biochemical constraint helps explain why some infants showed persistently poor clot clearance despite high CSF rtPA levels and prolonged intraventricular residence times ref [58], ref [9].

More aggressive strategies combined drainage with fibrinolysis and irrigation. In the DRIFT program, early phase studies suggested reduced shunt rates relative to historical cohorts and later follow-up indicated improved cognitive outcomes in survivors, yet the randomized trial did not reduce the short-term composite of shunt or death and was complicated by excess secondary intraventricular bleeding ref [10], ref [11], ref [12]. Overall, fibrinolysis can reopen CSF pathways under selected conditions, but its clinical utility remains constrained by timing, substrate availability, and hemorrhagic safety; current evidence supports it as an informative but not established nonsurgical therapy for routine posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus prevention ref [58], ref [9], ref [11], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Neuroprotective and Regenerative Approaches in Hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Hydrocephalus produces a robust neuroinflammatory milieu characterized by reactive astrocytosis, microgliosis, ependymal injury, white-matter distortion, and secondary disturbances of axonal connectivity rather than massive primary neuronal loss ref [65]. This profile makes anti-inflammatory and glial-modulating therapy conceptually attractive: activated microglia can amplify neuronal death through cytokine release, oxidative injury, and phagocytic programs, whereas astroglial scarring may worsen tissue compliance and impede repair ref [59], ref [65].

The best-developed pharmacologic evidence in hydrocephalus centers on minocycline, a pleiotropic tetracycline with anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, MMP-modulating, and microglia-suppressive actions ref [64]. In congenital H-Tx rats, minocycline significantly reduced GFAP-positive astrocytes and Iba1-positive microglia, with partial preservation of cortical thickness, supporting attenuation of established gliosis rather than simple developmental delay ref [60]. Comparable findings were reported in kaolin-induced rat hydrocephalus, where minocycline lowered GFAP and Iba1 expression and modestly slowed ventriculomegaly progression ref [61]. Broader rodent meta-analytic data in neurodegeneration reinforce that these effects are biologically plausible across disease contexts, although dose-response relationships are narrow and toxicity windows remain relevant ref [66].

Beyond minocycline, pathway-specific anti-cytokine approaches remain preliminary but notable. In a rabbit kaolin model, infliximab lowered CSF and serum TNF-alpha and reduced TUNEL-positive cells in the lateral geniculate body and optic radiations, suggesting protection of vulnerable visual pathways despite persistent hydrocephalus ref [63]. By contrast, anti-inflammatory interventions in TGF-beta1-overexpressing hydrocephalic mice reduced glial activation yet failed to reverse thioflavin-positive vascular deposits, and pioglitazone paradoxically worsened hydrocephalus, underscoring that suppressing gliosis does not necessarily normalize CSF dynamics or vascular pathology ref [62]. Overall, current data support glial modulation as an adjunctive neuroprotective strategy, but not a substitute for CSF diversion or causal correction.

subsections.section_title: Neuroprotective and Regenerative Approaches in Hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Oxidative stress is a plausible secondary injury mechanism in hydrocephalus, particularly within hypoperfused periventricular white matter. In young kaolin-induced models, direct evidence includes increased lipid peroxidation, nitrite production, and nitrotyrosine accumulation, with relatively weak endogenous antioxidant compensation, supporting a rationale for antioxidant intervention rather than purely CSF-directed therapy ref [67].

Small-molecule antioxidant studies have yielded mixed but conceptually informative results. Epigallocatechin gallate reduced malondialdehyde levels in periventricular white matter in infantile hydrocephalic rats, suggesting attenuation of free-radical mediated membrane injury ref [68]. Earlier work with N-acetylcysteine similarly lowered cerebral lipid peroxidation in experimental infantile hydrocephalus, reinforcing oxidative damage as a drug-responsive target. However, a broader oral antioxidant cocktail containing tocopherol, ascorbate, coenzyme Q10, glutathione, and lipoic acid failed to improve ventriculomegaly, behavior, gliosis, or myelin-related readouts despite some normalization of antioxidant capacity, indicating that biomarker improvement does not necessarily translate into structural rescue ref [69].

Beyond classical antioxidants, mechanistically targeted neuroprotection has focused on excitotoxicity and hemorrhage-related oxidative injury. Memantine is attractive because moderate-affinity NMDA receptor blockade may suppress pathological calcium influx while preserving physiological signaling ref [71]. In infantile rat hydrocephalus, memantine protected hippocampal neurons ref [72], and in hydrocephalic rabbits memantine, alone or with Morinda citrifolia, attenuated fourth-ventricle periventricular injury ref [73]. In related posthemorrhagic paradigms, edaravone reduced edema, lipid peroxidation, and later cognitive deficits after intraventricular hemorrhage, supporting free-radical scavenging as a potentially relevant adjunct for hemorrhage-associated hydrocephalus ref [70]. Overall, this literature suggests biological plausibility but only modest and model-dependent efficacy, with insufficient evidence that antioxidant or small-molecule neuroprotection can yet replace definitive CSF diversion.

subsections.section_title: Neuroprotective and Regenerative Approaches in Hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Regenerative and developmental preventive strategies in hydrocephalus seek to interrupt injury cascades before fixed ventricular enlargement and cortical dysgenesis emerge. Developmental studies strongly implicate prenatal hemorrhagic signaling as an initiating event rather than a mere association: lysophosphatidic acid exposure in fetal mice reproduced ventricular dilation, cortical thinning, ependymal loss, and ventricular zone disorganization, whereas LPA1 antagonism or receptor deletion reduced this phenotype, suggesting a tractable preventive target in fetal hydrocephalus ref [74]. Human autopsy data support the same causal axis, as apparently “cryptic” fetal intraventricular hemorrhage can obstruct the aqueduct with organizing blood products and hemosiderin-laden macrophages despite nondiagnostic antenatal imaging ref [75]. Together, these observations frame prevention not simply as CSF diversion avoidance, but as early interruption of hemorrhage-triggered developmental injury ref [74], ref [75].

A distinct developmental-preventive line comes from folate biology in the hydrocephalic Texas rat. Altered fetal CSF folate handling, including abnormalities in folate-metabolizing enzymes, was linked to impaired progenitor proliferation; importantly, maternal supplementation with tetrahydrofolate plus folinic acid reduced hydrocephalus incidence and improved cortical growth, whereas folic acid alone worsened incidence in this model ref [78]. These findings are provocative because they suggest that targeted metabolic correction, rather than generic supplementation, may modify susceptibility during a narrow fetal window ref [78]. Although translation to humans remains unproven, the work highlights the need to consider hydrocephalus as a disorder of disturbed developmental signaling as much as of fluid mechanics ref [78].

Cell-based repair has been explored most extensively in posthemorrhagic neonatal models. Human umbilical cord blood-derived mesenchymal stem cells reduced ventricular enlargement, inflammatory cytokines, gliosis, cell death, and white-matter injury after severe intraventricular hemorrhage in newborn rats, thereby preventing posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus in a subset of studies ref [79]. Subsequent route-comparison experiments suggested that intracerebroventricular delivery achieved higher local engraftment, but intravenous administration produced broadly comparable protection in this permeable-barrier setting, with mannitol adding little benefit ref [7]. These data support a primarily paracrine, immunomodulatory mechanism rather than true tissue replacement ref [79], ref [7]. Beyond direct hydrocephalus endpoints, adjunct systemic neurorestorative strategies may still matter: erythropoietin improved long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in extremely preterm infants, particularly among those with intraventricular hemorrhage, even though it was not designed as a hydrocephalus-specific therapy ref [8]. Overall, regenerative and developmental prevention remains conceptually compelling, but requires rigorous validation for timing, dose, route, safety, and phenotype-specific efficacy before clinical adoption ref [78], ref [79], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Neuroprotective and Regenerative Approaches in Hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
A sobering feature of the hydrocephalus neuroprotection literature is that several mechanistically plausible agents have failed when tested in established animal models. In young rats with kaolin-induced hydrocephalus, chronic tacrolimus and cyclosporine A did not improve behavior, ventricular enlargement, or white-matter injury, and calcineurin inhibition was accompanied by biochemical and histological evidence of renal toxicity; calpain inhibition was likewise ineffective ref [80]. Similarly, mexiletine and riluzole, despite rationale based on calcium-dependent axonal injury, produced no meaningful behavioral, structural, or biochemical benefit in kaolin hydrocephalus ref [81]. These negative studies are important because they argue against assuming that axon-directed neuroprotection in hydrocephalus will mirror efficacy seen in trauma or ischemia models ref [80], ref [81].

Such results support a more modest, adjunctive view of nonsurgical therapy: pharmacologic measures may at best bridge the preshunt period, reduce secondary injury, or target specific etiologic subtypes, rather than replace cerebrospinal fluid diversion ref [85]. Del Bigio's laboratory perspective emphasized that hydrocephalus injury is multifactorial—mechanical distortion, hypoperfusion, altered extracellular homeostasis, and impaired development—so single-target agents are unlikely to be broadly transformative ref [85]. This framing also helps explain why positive signals in experimental neuroprotection often fail to generalize clinically, a problem long recognized in stroke research, where timing, model severity, publication bias, and overreliance on surrogate outcomes inflate preclinical promise ref [7], ref [8], ref [9].

Accordingly, translational progress in hydrocephalus will require more rigorous preclinical standards: randomization, blinding, prespecified outcomes, adequate power, negative-result reporting, and testing across ages, comorbidities, and model types ref [8], ref [9]. The broader stroke literature has shown both the sheer volume of apparently successful preclinical interventions and the poor correlation between experimental enthusiasm and clinical benefit ref [7], ref [9]. For hydrocephalus, this argues for prioritizing therapies with clear mechanistic linkage to disease stage, demonstrable CNS exposure, acceptable systemic safety, and realistic positioning as supportive or preventive adjuncts to surgery rather than stand-alone alternatives ref [80], ref [81], ref [85].
